items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' or offered any warm-up. The opener was 'Alright, we this is Chris. How can I help you?' and the second line was 'Okay, what day you're looking at done?' — a returning customer who had just moved with Einstein three weeks earlier got no acknowledgment of that until she raised it herself.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The call had genuine complexity — two cities, two days, a packing job, an overnight truck hold — and none of that structure was previewed. The customer had to guess what was coming, which is why she interrupted mid-plan with 'If that's not how it needs to work, I just need the plan for her to go ahead and come here and stay with us.'

The prior move was never used. She opened with 'you guys did a move from me end of a August' and said 'I should be in your system cause you all just moved up,' and the entire response was 'Yeah, for, for sure. I was just making sure.' Her actual hours, her actual crew, and what she paid last time were all sitting in the record and would have made every number on this call more credible.
Additional rooms never asked — no garage, no storage unit, no patio or balcony question, on a job where Einstein is doing the packing and therefore owns every cabinet and closet in the unit.

Special considerations never probed — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns. The customer said the origin is 'real easy to get in and out, it's one story' and Chris took that at face value rather than asking what the walk from the truck to the door actually is at a senior independent living facility.

Access concerns never asked, and this is the most expensive miss on the call. The origin is a senior independent living community — 'she lives in a senior independent living. She has two it's like a condo... it's half of a duplex.' Facilities like that routinely require a certificate of insurance, a reserved move-out window, gate access, and a check-in at a front office. Chris booked an 8:30 arrival on two consecutive days without asking about any of it. If the facility turns the crew away at the gate on October 12th, the packing day is lost and the Winnsboro drive on the 13th collapses with it.

The moving-stressor question was never asked. This is an elderly woman being relocated 137 miles away from her independent living community to her family's house — a genuinely emotional move — and no one asked what anybody was worried about.

What's-included was never stated at all. Not gas, not the truck, not taxes, not insurance, not wrap, pads, bands, or tools. The $194/hour number was delivered bare. On a two-day, 137-mile job where the truck sits loaded overnight at the Fort Worth office, 'what am I actually paying for' is not a rhetorical question.

Disassembly and reassembly was never framed as included. It surfaced only as a scheduling caveat — 'obviously if she's staying there then they wouldn't, you know, disassemble or prep the bad' — so the customer heard it as a service that might or might not happen rather than a no-extra-cost inclusion, on a job with two beds and a chest of drawers.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The load includes a cherry TV cabinet and an entire elderly woman's household, and it spends a night locked on a truck in a yard in Fort Worth before driving two hours and sixteen minutes to Winnsboro. There is no call in this sample where $2,000 of repair-replace-reimburse coverage would have been more reassuring, and it was never said.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — on a job where the customer is not the person being moved. Her mother-in-law is the one who opens the door to strangers on packing day. The pre-move email with the movers' names and photos is built for exactly this situation.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite Chris committing to '8:30 arrival time for the crew' on two consecutive days with a 137-mile drive hanging off the second one.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch and no 'pricing is super simple' opener. The closest was 'the only additional cost of the hourly and a transportation fee would be the packing materials,' which scopes the fees but never makes the no-credit-card-fee / no-fuel-surcharge / no-assembly-fee claim.

The clock explanation was half-built. Fifteen-minute proration landed — 'ultimately you pay for the time use in fifteen minute increments. So if they get it done quicker... then you're paying less' — but the 2.5-hour minimum was never stated and neither was when the clock starts. On a two-day job that is two separate billing events, the customer has no idea whether day one has a floor under it.
Specialty items never asked — no piano, safe, antique or artwork question. On a senior's household being packed by the crew, heirlooms are likely and their handling time is real.
Walk distance never asked at either end. The Winnsboro destination is a rural house on a county road and nobody established where the truck can park.

The packing-materials figure came out unusable: 'it sounds like, there'll be the about a two bedroom worth probably anywhere from like $1.01505 million and packing materials.' Whatever the intended number was, the customer never received it — and it is one of only three line items on a $3,344 estimate.

Save Your Ass speech largely absent. Chris reached the right idea once — 'they can definitely use those first, so you're spending lesser' on her twenty to thirty existing boxes — but never delivered the prep logic that prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill, never gave consolidation examples, and never offered the carload tip. On a two-day job billed at $194/hour across thirteen estimated hours, every fifteen minutes the family can absorb themselves is $48.50.
No deposit required was never mentioned. She committed to two full days in October, three weeks out, on a call where nobody told her it costs nothing to hold them.

No bolded-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. 'I'll send you a confirmation email with all those details' plus 'If any changes on your end, you can call, text or email us' is a change-notification channel, not a request to check the record. On a two-date, two-address, three-line-item job with a $672 transportation fee and a garbled materials number, the verification ask is not optional.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The call went from booking confirmation straight to 'Alright, thanks Deborah, we'll talk to you soon.'
No hours and no direct number given — 'you can call, text or email us' with nothing attached to it.

Customer's name used twice — once while typing it into the profile and once in the farewell. Short of the 3+ standard, and never used during the plan negotiation where it would have done the most work.
top_strength: Chris's handling of the two-day structure is the strongest operational thinking in this week's sample, and he did it in real time without getting defensive when the customer pushed back on his first answer. He opened by sizing the actual constraint out loud: 'it says a 137 miles about two hours and sixteen minutes give or take to get from hills to your house and then so with the drive, it'd probably be something where we would pack and load everything in one day obviously and then keep it locked on our truck overnight at our Fort Worth office and then drive and unload the following day. Does that sound pretty much a you envisioned?' That is a complete logistics plan with a sense-check attached, delivered before the customer asked for one. When she said no — 'I was hoping you all could pack it on that Monday and then load it and bring it on Tuesday. If that's not how it needs to work, I just need the plan for her to go ahead and come here and stay with us' — he reversed cleanly and immediately: 'Oh, no, I mean we can do it that way too. Either way you're.' No friction, no re-selling his version. He then rebuilt the numbers to match her plan on the fly: 'the packing portion itself of packing prep and everything would probably only take anywhere from like four to five hours... and then the following day, it'd be more of a generally locally a two bedroom move. Like this from a first floor to a house takes anywhere from... four to six hours, you add in the two and a half hour drive and so be close to a full day eight hours or so.' That is a rep decomposing an unusual job into billable components and pricing each one in front of the customer — packing hours, move hours, drive time, the $672 transportation fee, and materials — and arriving at a number she accepted without hesitation. He also used a real-world equivalent to settle the truck question, which almost nobody does: she said her husband's move 'all fit in a 28 foot trail truck' and Chris anchored to it — 'Yeah. It's about the size of our trucks we I would expect him to go outside of one truck.' And he found her money without being asked, on her own boxes: 'Oh, yeah, they can definitely use those first, so you're spending lesser.' The booking attempt was direct and it closed: 'Okay, did you want to go ahead and book it ten for those days?'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Chris built and closed a genuinely complicated two-day, two-city, $3,344 job and delivered almost none of the reasons Einstein is worth it. Section 3 came in at 8/20 — no what's-included list, no No Worries Damage Coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no hidden-fees pitch — on the one call in this sample where all four would have landed hardest. Her mother-in-law's entire household spends a night locked on a truck in a Fort Worth yard before a 137-mile drive. 'Everything's covered while it's on our truck — every move comes with our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse, and that's included, not an add-on. Most companies give you sixty cents a pound.' That is thirty seconds and it is the single most reassuring thing anyone could say on this call. Same for Meet Your Mover: Deborah is not the person opening the door on packing day, her mother-in-law is, so 'a few days out we'll email you the crew's names and photos so she knows exactly who's showing up' answers a question the family has not asked yet. Second priority: the senior living facility. Chris booked two 8:30 arrivals without asking a single access question about a building type that almost always has a certificate-of-insurance requirement, a reserved move-out window, and a front desk. That is not a scoring nitpick — it is the most likely way this booking fails on October 12th, and the packing day failing takes the Winnsboro drive down with it. Add three questions to every facility or complex job: does the building need a COI from us, do we need to reserve a window or an elevator, and where can the truck actually park. Third, finish the clock. Proration landed, the 2.5-hour minimum and the clock-start trigger did not, and on a two-day job that is two separate billing events with two separate floors — the customer should know that before move day, not on the invoice. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: Chris said the padding out loud — 'We try to, you know, shoot conservatively. So the only surprise is you're paying less.' That framing is exactly the habit driving the 45-46% number, because it makes over-quoting feel like customer service. His actual ranges also drifted within the same two minutes: packing went 'four to five hours. If that's maybe not even that,' then 'four to six hours,' and settled at five; the move-day leg went 'four to six hours' plus 'two and a half hour drive,' and settled at eight. Both landed at or near the top of his own stated ranges, then got described as conservative. Worth pulling the actuals on both days when this runs in October — a two-bedroom senior's unit with no appliances, a two-person dining table, and the crew's own boxes already staged is a strong candidate for coming in well under five hours on packing day. Finally, he has a completed sale and no verification loop. Two dates, two addresses, a $672 transportation fee and a materials number that came out of his mouth as '$1.01505 million' — send the email with the details bolded at the top and say 'read it over and reply with any corrections.' That is the fix for exactly the kind of number this call produced.
phone_presence_notes: Easy to deal with and completely non-defensive — he reversed his own plan the moment she pushed back ('Oh, no, I mean we can do it that way too') and never once made her feel like she was making it harder — but the warmth stayed procedural: no 'how are you,' no acknowledgment that she had just moved with Einstein three weeks earlier, her name used twice, and a long run of bare 'Okay. Okay. Okay' acknowledgments with several false starts talking over her.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence that cannot be trusted on its own. Chris's lines are unusually fragmented with what looks like heavy crosstalk — 'Okay, and what should I so that you're good to send you so I can put Deborah whet as the name on the job or the con, the profile or okay,' 'a two bedroom move. Like this from a first floor to a house takes anywhere from the 5:00 or six at 4:00 to six hours' — and the packing-materials figure renders as '$1.01505 million.' Audio is needed to tell whether he is genuinely talking over the customer and garbling numbers or whether this is a bad transcription of a fast but clear delivery, and specifically to recover what he actually quoted for packing materials.
